newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries close lower ahead of FOMC meeting.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries close lower ahead of FOMC meeting.

text.p: The prices of U.S. Treasury securities ended lower as market participants awaited the results of Tuesday's Federal Reserve meeting.

The Fed's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee meets on Tuesday and analysts were split as to whether it would vote to further tighten monetary policy. Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan has stated the central bank would raise short-term interest rates again if economic growth continued at the rapid pace seen in the fourth quarter of 1996 and first quarter of this year.
The FOMC voted to raise the federal funds rate by 25 basis points at its last meeting on March 25. Under Greenspan's tutelage the Fed has not moved to tighten or lower interest rates only once.
"It's becoming a muddied field. We've seen a very large rise in short-term interest rates in the last couple of days," said Hugh Johnson, chief economist at First Albany Corp.
"I said on Friday that economists and strategists were convinced the Fed would not move. But investors are (betting the Fed will tighten monetary policy)," and I'll take their opinion," Johnson said.
Johnson said that on the 15 of May the yield on the three-month Treasury bill was 5.11 percent, and had now risen to 5.30 percent.
"That is a very substantial rise in short-term interest rates," Johnson said. In late trading on Monday the Treasury's three-month bill was up 10 basis points from Friday's close.
"My sense is we'll see a range ahead of the announcement. But we're not out of the woods yet," said Kathleen Stephansen, senior economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp.
Gross domestic product and the May nonfarm payrolls report were still due, meaning any rally likely would be short-lived, Stephanson said.
Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc., said it was a tough call on whether the Fed would raise interest rates, though he expected it would.
There seemed to be a change of heart after the weekend on what course the Fed would pursue, Low said.
Otherwise, it would be a slow week, Low said.
The only potentially market-moving number he saw was initial jobless claims on Thursday.
"It would be hard to dismiss" another weak reading in initial claims, Low said. Claims slipped dramatically last week, another sign of labor market tightness.

Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan has stated that he will look to continued signals of strong economic growth to further tighten monetary policy -- even if no blatant statistics surfaced in official economic reports.

The 30-year bond was off 5/32 at 96-10 to yield 6.92 percent. The 10-year note closed at 99-13/32, down 2/32 to yield 6.71 percent. Five-year notes ended at 100-08/32, down 5/32 to yield 6.56 percent.
Near the shorter end of the maturity range, two-year notes closed at 100-6/32, down 1/32 to yield 6.27 percent.
Three-month bill rates rose 11 basis points to 5.17 percent. Six-month bill rates rose seven basis points to 5.40 percent. Year bill rates rose two basis points to 5.55 percent.
